question.text: Chenab Infrastructure Trust (Cat I-IIF) has set up a Limited Partner Advisory Committee (LPAC). Which of the following BEST describes the LPAC's typical governance role?

answer.text: LPAC has binding investment-approval authority — it replaces the Manager's Investment Committee
LPAC is a SEBI-mandated committee that must include the Trustee as Chair
LPAC functions as the external audit committee and signs off on annual financials

LPAC is an advisory body comprising representatives of major LPs that reviews conflicts of interest, valuation matters, key-person events and amendments to the LPA; it provides advisory (generally non-binding) input but does NOT make individual investment decisions

explanation.text: **The Logic:** An LPAC (Limited Partner Advisory Committee) is a governance body of major LP representatives that advises the Manager on matters like conflicts of interest (related-party transactions, co-investment conflicts), valuation escalations, key-person events, extensions of fund term, and amendments to the LPA/PPM. LPAC input is generally non-binding on investment selection (that's the Manager's IC responsibility) but is weighty on governance and conflict issues. **The Trap:** The binding-IC-replacement option confuses LPAC with the Investment Committee. The SEBI-mandated/Trustee-chair option invents a composition (LPAC is contractually set up, not regulator-mandated). The audit-committee option confuses with statutory auditor. **Cross-Exam Context:** XIX-C covers LPAC. XIX-A (Cat I/II Distributor) may test LP-rights disclosures including LPAC access. In US/Cayman funds, LPAC is also called LPAC or Advisory Board — same concept. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Draft LPAC terms carefully in the LPA: clearly distinguish consent matters (e.g., conflict waivers, related-party deals) from consultation matters (strategy review). Rotate LPAC seats by LP commitment size to avoid giving any single LP de facto control. Minute every LPAC meeting — these are your audit trail in disputes.
